title: The mind comes first (1–2)
hook: all that we are is the result of what we have thought; pain follows an evil thought as the wheel follows the ox

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened the Dhammapada: four hundred twenty-three verses, twenty-six chapters. Your line was the path, in verses. Which chapter title pulled at you? Day one hundred fifty-eight, and verse one.

Picture an ox cart on a dirt road in ancient India. The ox leans into the yoke and steps forward. Behind it, the heavy wooden wheel turns and follows, rut by rut, wherever the ox goes. The wheel has no say. It can't choose a different road. Everyone in the Buddha's world had watched that a thousand times. And the first verse of the Dhammapada takes that ordinary sight and says: this is how your life works. Today: the mind comes first.
screen: `AN OX CART ON A DIRT ROAD.` → `THE WHEEL HAS NO SAY.` → `THIS IS HOW YOUR LIFE WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here is verse one in Max Müller's English: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.” Verse two is its twin, the same shape with one change: if someone speaks or acts with a pure thought, “happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.” That's why chapter one is called the twin verses. The pairs mirror each other: the wheel and the shadow, pain and happiness. Müller's opening line is famous, but the Pali is even more direct. It says, roughly: mind goes before all things; mind is their chief; they are made by mind. Mind comes first. Speech and action follow. And what follows carries the quality of the mind it came from. The old commentary tells a story for verse one. A blind monk named Cakkhupala walked up and down one night and stepped on many insects. Other monks were shocked: he'd killed living things. The Buddha said no. He didn't see them, and he didn't intend it. There was no evil thought behind the step. For this tradition, what matters is the intention the act comes from. That's why the verse starts with the mind, not the deed. This isn't a promise that thinking happy thoughts fixes everything. It's closer to a warning, and an invitation. What you set going in the mind will be pulled along behind you. And you can watch the ox before the wheel starts to turn.
screen: `VERSE ONE: THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.` · `VERSE TWO: THE SHADOW THAT STAYS.` · `THE PALI: MIND GOES BEFORE ALL.` · `THE BLIND MONK: NO INTENT, NO FAULT.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath find its own pace. Now watch for the ox. A thought will come: a worry, a plan, a memory. Before you get carried off by it, notice what it's doing to your mood. Does the chest tighten? Does the face soften? Is there a small lift, or a small sinking? You don't have to change anything. Just see the thought step forward, and feel the wheel of your mood begin to follow. Then come back to the breath and wait for the next one. The bell holds the time.
Manopubbangama. Having mind as forerunner: the Dhammapada's first two verses, where mind goes before all, and words and deeds follow, like a wheel or a shadow.
Your line: the wheel follows the ox. Today, catch one thought steering your mood, and see where it was about to pull you. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: The opening verses of the Dhammapada are among the most often chanted and memorized Buddhist verses; teachers use them to explain that intention (cetana) shapes action and its results.

match.prompt: match the pieces of verses one and two.
pairs: the blind monk who stepped on insects

myth: the Dhammapada says that thinking happy thoughts fixes everything
it says what the mind sets going follows you; it's closer to a warning and an invitation.
in the commentary, the Buddha said the blind monk wasn't at fault for the insects
he didn't see them and didn't intend it; intention is what counts.
the Pali says, roughly, mind goes before all things
Müller's 'all that we are is the result of what we have thought' is a looser, famous rendering.

fork.setup: a blind monk has stepped on insects in the dark. the other monks want him blamed for killing. you're the Buddha. what do you say?
options: he broke the precept; he's at fault.
he didn't see them or intend it; there's no fault.
fork.reveal: in the commentary the Buddha clears him: no intention to kill, no evil thought, so no evil deed.

original.note: Pali: 'having mind as their forerunner,' the first word of the Dhammapada.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'all that we are is the result of what we have thought' means positive thinking.
what it means: mind goes before speech and action, and what follows carries the quality of the mind it came from.
what a scholar hears: 'manopubbangama dhamma' is debated: dhamma here may mean mental states or all experiences; Müller's rendering is famously free.

sources.quoted: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.
happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.

notes: Check verses 1 and 2 against Müller's SBE 10 (1881) text word for word.
The Cakkhupala story is simplified: the commentary goes on to explain his blindness by a past-life deed; only the intention point is told here.
The Pali rendering 'mind goes before all things; mind is their chief; they are made by mind' is a paraphrase, not a quotation.
Close screen title uses the index title's head without the verse numbers.
